dataSheet.description: A generic dual-motor electric crossover in the 2.1 t class: roughly 300 kW, 2.9 m wheelbase, a floor-mounted battery for a low centre of mass, near 50/50 weight distribution, single-speed reduction gears.
sources: Class-typical figures from manufacturer specification sheets for mid-size electric crossovers (mass 2000–2250 kg, wheelbase 2.85–2.95 m, Cd 0.26–0.29, centre of mass 0.5–0.55 m, 51/49 front weight bias).
Tire feel parameters tuned to a ~0.9 g skidpad and ~37 m 100–0 km/h braking distance on all-season tires, in the range of published road tests for the class.
Suspension rates for ~1.5 Hz front and ~1.6 Hz rear ride frequencies (Gillespie ch. 5), roll centres of a strut front near 80 mm and a multilink rear near 130 mm (Milliken & Milliken ch. 17).

Drivetrain [ILLUSTRATIVE]: two motors modelled as one unit of 520 N·m and 300 kW to 16 000 rpm through a 9:1 reduction, torque split evenly through an open centre differential, 90 N·m of lift-off regeneration. An electric motor's torque is instant, so the preset ships with traction control on, as every production EV does (ADR-0013).
Steering geometry [ILLUSTRATIVE]: 6° of caster (about 28 mm of trail), a small scrub radius and strong electric assist; aero after Hucho ch. 4, a smooth body with a little front lift.

Travel curves [ILLUSTRATIVE] (ADR-0026): roll-centre height falling with bump and camber gain at rates scaled from the curves derived for Project Chrono's BMW E90 from its hardpoints (MacPherson front: roll centre −2.9 mm per mm of bump, camber about −20°/m; double wishbone: −1.6 mm per mm; docs/validation/chrono-bmw-e90.md), eased for this car's lower roll centres. No toe curves: road cars are set up for near-zero bump steer, and the E90 comparison found toe follows force more than travel.
dataSheet.notes: Not a specific production model. The two motors share one torque curve in this format; the centre differential's torque split stands in for the independent rear-biased control a real dual-motor car has.
